title: The 6 Rules of UI Cards
summary: This lesson outlines a systematic approach to designing UI cards, focusing on treatment based on background, single-entity logic, and avoiding common pitfalls like nesting. It provides specific rules for clickability, aspect ratios in grids, and adapting card styles for dark mode.

transcript.text: Cards are a system. Border, shadow, or flat. The background decides.
A card is one entity. One title, one subject, one place to go.
Cards for everything is the AI-made tell. A form section is not a card.
Border on white, shadow on tinted, flat inside a panel. The background picks the treatment.
On white, a shadow barely reads. On grey, a border is noise.
A clickable card is clickable everywhere. One action, the whole surface.
Two buttons inside means it is not a card, it is a panel. Hover lifts the whole thing.
Never nest cards. A card inside a card is a box inside a box. Flatten the inner one. Dividers do the grouping.
Media inside cards keeps one aspect ratio across the grid. 16 by 9 on every card. Cropped, never stretched. One tall image and the row breaks.
Dark mode kills shadows. Borders come back. One step lighter than the surface. Elevation becomes surface tint.

Six decisions. One card that knows its background. Now make Claude Code think like a senior UX designer. UX Engine designs the screen before coding, audits what is broken, reviews the diff, and kills the AI look. Link in bio.

on_screen_text: Six decisions. One card that knows its background.
design_principles: Single-entity principle (one title, one subject, one destination)
Single-action clickability (entire surface as a button)
Avoidance of card nesting (use dividers instead)
Consistent aspect ratios (16:9) to prevent grid row breaks
Dark mode elevation through tinting and borders rather than shadows
before_after: Shows the transformation of a complex panel with nested cards and multiple buttons into a clean, single-entity card with internal dividers and a single clickable surface.
